utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Welcome to everyone in the courtroom. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, since you are on your feet, I take it that you would like to bring something to the attention of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, good day. Good day to everyone. Yes, very briefly. The Defence counsel has tried to prepare what was necessary for the witness who will be examined in a minute, but we have to emphasise the following: A lot of documents were submitted to the Defence counsel and we didn't have much time and we think that -- if we think that the rhythm of this procedure will be correct, we hope that we might start the cross-examination when the time comes, but the Defence would appreciate it if it were possible for the Defence to call this witness back later, at a convenient time, once it has conferred with General Galic, which we haven't been able to do yet. We haven't been able to confer with General Galic, and I would like to underline that. You are aware of the reasons, they are technical reasons, not something over which the Defence has any power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Piletta-Zanin had courteously informed me before today's session that that was his position. I am grateful for that. The documents which the Prosecution proposes to tender had all been disclosed -- documents which had all been disclosed by the 6th of February, some of them as early as April 2001. I hasten to add, however, that the translations of the documents were not provided until this week, some of them only yesterday. However, I anticipate that during examination-in-chief the relevant portions of the documents will, in almost all cases, be a sentence or a few words, even less than a sentence. Occasionally, maybe two sentences. In other words, although my friend is correct when he says he has a bundle of documents - I think there are around 16 or thereabouts, perhaps 20 - there will not be much of a document that will be relevant. Mr. President, the witness has come from Canada. If it is possible without prejudice to the Defence, given the lateness of the provision of the translations, if it is possible without prejudice for the Defence to complete its cross-examination tomorrow, then the Prosecution, and I am sure the witness, will be very grateful for that, rather than bringing him back at some later date. Perhaps could I respectfully suggest that the Defence waits until examination-in-chief is concluded because they may then be greatly assisted in their assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until now, Mr. Ierace, I didn't hear anything else that the Defence reserved the right. That means that they are already waiting and seeing how things will develop and then we will see whether they use.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. In fact, we are ready, but only partially, very partially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see. The experience has shown us that sometimes things are going unexpectedly smoother and sometimes they go less smooth. It's I wouldn't say always, but sometimes looking back, we spend a lot of time on issues that were not that much issues any more when we came to the point that we had to actually deal with the matters. So, therefore, I understand the position of both parties. Would the Prosecution be ready to call, as I understand, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and he will be taken by Mr. Mundis. Just one remaining matter in relation to Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I interrupted you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And that is his exhibits are, in fact, confidential exhibits. I apologise for not having specifically set out that in the letter. They all do carry our ERN numbers. Excuse me, Mr. President. I think, with the exception of rather six documents, they are confidential exhibits. Mr. President, might I be excused since Mr. Mundis is taking Mr. Thomas? And if I am required back in the Trial Chamber during the course of the day, of course, I will be here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mundis, will you keep a close eye on what are protected documents and what are not protected documents? It is mainly the, I take it, the relationship between the Prosecution as the receiving party of the information and it is not the personal protection of the witness but it is, rather, a functional protection of the witness and documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President, and I would attempt to, once we get to the point where we need to deal with these documents, to deal with all of them, even though it might not be the most logical way of doing that because we will, pursuant to the provider's request, we will ask to go into closed session to discuss the documents and we would respectfully, at that point, request that of the Trial Chamber. And we will attempt to deal with them all at one time, even though that may not seem logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will also have in the back of your mind that if private session would be good enough, that at least keep some of the public character of this trial open.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Since Mr. Ierace will be leaving, one of the series of questions that we intend to ask the witness about this, and he knows a lot about this and this is why I mentioned this a while ago, it had to do with the relation between the warring factions and the press and perhaps it also had to do with the manipulation of information or the manipulation of documents. And I would very much appreciate it if we could address this today since we are almost at the end of the week. It is the day before the deadline that you have fixed for the Prosecution. If you could tell me before the hearing of the witness what the reply of the Prosecution will be to what I have called "deletion or manipulation of documents." I think this is important for us to establish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a request directed to you, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think on the last occasion, Mr. President, Mr. Stamp dealt with this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we either wanted to have final answer or a detailed description of the efforts undertaken, and I have to look back in the transcript in what detail the information was provided because we got a direct answer then on what happened. I would have to look it up in order to be sure whether that is the degree of detail which would be proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you require either myself or Mr. Stamp at the beginning of the next session to be present, should there be any further query in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will discuss the matter and I have a look at the transcript as well, and then we will let you know whether your presence is wished by the Court or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Usher could you please bring Mr. -- the next witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text of the declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I, Francis Roy Thomas, solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thomas. Please be seated. You will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, where are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I am self-employed as a peace support training operations consultant, and that has taken me to Ecuador, Thailand, Switzerland, Sweden, Canada, itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to commencing your consultant, were you a member of the Canadian Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I was -- had 35 years of service as a tank and armoured reconnaissance and I also did -- served in seven UN missions during that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber your educational background throughout the course of your military career.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I attend the Pakistan Army Command and Staff College. I attended the Canadian Forces Command and Staff College. I have taken Masters in War Studies at Royal Military College. I spent one year at the United Kingdom tank technology course. I can elaborate further, if the Court desires, on my UN tours as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could briefly tell us which UN tours you participated in?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I participated in Cyprus as a reconnaissance commander. I was a military observer both on the Golan Heights --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I am very sorry, Mr. President, but I can see the witness has mentioned tank technology and this hasn't appeared in the French transcript. I think that he is speaking too rapidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not been listening to the French channel, but the speed of your speech is such that the translators cannot translate all the words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise this. As a Canadian, I should recognise this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will not interfere in Canadian language experiences, Mr. Southwell, but if you would please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will go back. Do you want me to repeat again my education?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think especially the -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, since I didn't follow it --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The fact that the translation forgot something is not that important, but we can go back to the passage, to what the witness said when he spoke about his academic experience. This was not completely caught by the French cabin, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will just asking the witness who is -- I would say your academic education, if you would repeat from that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I attended the Pakistan Army Command and Staff College. I attended the Canadian Army Command and Staff College. I completed a Masters in War Study at the Royal Military College. I also attended a one-year tank technology course in the United Kingdom, and probably for the edification of this Court, I could add at this time some additional qualifications. I also have a NATO background in electronic warfare. I have taken a NATO course in nuclear biological chemical defence. I have German and Canadian parachute qualifications, and I have a United Kingdom joint operations training. To go back to -- was that -- did the translators in French catch that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will follow the French channel and see whether...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wish to make sure that I am speaking at the appropriate rate because they have a difficult job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether you were listening, but the French cabin said that questions and answers should not overlap. I think this is better for everyone. Could the witness please wait for the translation to be finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...before answering the question. And if Mr. Mundis would do approximately the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, could you please tell the Trial Chamber which UN tours you participated in?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: My first UN tour was in Cyprus, where I was a troop commandant with reconnaissance. My second tours were in the Middle East with -- on the Golan Heights and with South Lebanon. My next UN -- my next UN tour was in Afghanistan as a military observer. And I was a military observer in Macedonia, where I was a team leader in Ohrid, and then I was the senior United Nations military observer, which is of interest to this court, in Sector Sarajevo from October 1993 to July 1994. I will say again, I was the senior United Nations military observer in Sector Sarajevo from October 1993 to July 1994. I concluded -- my last UN tour was as Deputy Chief of Operations for the United Nations military component in Haiti, a force of 6.000. My final tour in the Canadian Forces was as the chief, the first -- my final UN tour in the Canadian Forces was as the first chief instructor of the Canadian Forces Peace Support Training Centre. I think that probably gives the Court an idea of my United Nations experience. Some other aspects of my military background that might have relevance to this Court setting, I should tell you, in the Canadian forces, reconnaissance troops are trained and expected to be able to call down artillery fire. I myself can tell you, this Court, that I have, as a junior officer, called down artillery fire. I have done a tour in our National Defence Headquarters as the responsible Canadian officer for the rapid reaction forces, both land and sea -- correction, land and air. The infantry battalion contribution to the Ace Mobile Force land, and also the Air Force squadron that flew F-18s to Central Europe. Another item of interest to this Court, I was involved in the contingency planning cell at our national headquarters, where I dealt with a crisis we had involving our native peoples, preparation and involvement with the Canadian Forces that served in the Gulf War, and I was also involved in the presenting the options for the Canadian contributions to Somalia, the former Yugoslavia, and some other UN missions. So this is background that might interest as well because it is involved with options and political considerations of the military components.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Might I ask if the usher could perhaps move the ELMO. I am having a difficult time seeing the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, I would like to focus your attention on your assignment as Senior Military Observer, Sector Sarajevo. Do you recall the date, the specific date, in October 1993 that you arrived and assumed those responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I can't be exactly sure. I think it was either 14 or 15 October, 1993. It was a Saturday, for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your primary duties and responsibilities as Senior Military Observer, Sector Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: My primary duty was to command and control and make sure that the people under my command carried out their functions as military observers, of the military observers assigned to Sector Sarajevo, which varied in numbers from 110 to almost 200. In fact, 223, I was told one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your tour in Sarajevo, how were the military observers that were assigned to your command distributed and allocated?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I had two teams which will be of little interest to this Court in Eastern Bosnian. I had a team of UNMOs, about 7 to 10, in the pocket of Zepa, and I had a team of 7 to 12 in the team of Gorazde. Within Sarajevo itself, the remainder of the UNMOs were broken initially into two teams, the Papa team which was found inside the city, and the Lima team, acquiring that name from Lima for "Lukavica," was on the Serb side. And I should add at this point - although I am sure previous witnesses have brought it out - that the only armed UNPROFOR troops allowed to operate in the Bosnian Serb area of operations in Sector Sarajevo were, in fact, those troops escorting convoys or on liaison tasks. So we were the only full-time UNPROFOR presence until the ceasefire of February 1994. The main function of my military observers was to monitor and report. And I know that the UNPROFOR mission was delivery of humanitarian aid, but you must bear in mind, my military observers were unarmed and they had no protective vehicles and no means of enforcing adherence to any agreement for delivery of humanitarian aid. But they could report, and that was their main function. They, of course, because they were the only UNPROFOR presence that lived full-time on the Bosnian Serb side, they affected a lot of liaison for all the UN agencies and not just the military component.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, to whom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you, as well, to make a pause because I hear the speed of the French translators and it really goes a bit too quick.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise. I just can't get used to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, to whom did you report as the Senior Military Observer, Sector Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I reported to two people. I was double hatted. I was under the operational control of the Commander, Sector Sarajevo. So for operations involving Sector Sarajevo, he, in fact, could give me direction, operational direction. But I also was under the command and the operational command of the Senior Military Observer for Bosnia-Herzegovina and the UN Senior Military Observer and, therefore, the Chief Military Observer for UNPROFOR in Zagreb. And I had two chains of command and I reported up both chains of command. And, obviously, if the sector commander asked me to do something which I felt was in contradiction with my other chain of command, that this would be an issue that would have to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, when you arrived in Sarajevo, whom did you relieve as senior military observer?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I relieved a Finnish lieutenant-colonel, Lieutenant Colonel Kukkola, a Finnish Engineer Officer. Now, he may, in fact, have another name now, I don't know. Somebody -- I haven't been in touch with him in years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many military observers were on the Papa side when you arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I would say about -- there were six teams, with five to -- it would be between 30 and 40. And the remaining teams would be on the Lima side, although I had a very small staff at my headquarters of about seven people when I first arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, focussing on the Papa side, when you say "six teams," did each of those teams operate out of an observation post?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: They operated out of what I would rather prefer to call a team base, which was situated so that it had good observation. Three of the team bases were sited so as to also offer observation back towards the city so they could observe the impact of shells or towards an area where they could observe an impact of shells. The other observation posts were not really correctly observation posts. One of them was in a house at the base of Mount Igman and that house was really, for all intents and purposes, a team base. And on Mount Igman itself, we had a team, and their main function when I arrived was to resolve an issue that had grown up out of the Mount Igman agreement of August. And, of course, the Papa headquarters itself was on the top floor of a four-storey apartment and it -- there was limited observation from that point but it was not in any sense an OP. It was as good an OP as you could get in a very urban setting in the low ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many Lima OPs existed at the time you arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. There would be six. I should make a point for the edification of the Court. One of the first things I did was to visit everyone in my OPs and spend at least one night sleeping overnight with each team, to meet the individuals at that site and to get to know them, and to get to know what the task was like from their particular vantage point. There was and, again, I know you probably have seen many maps and I feel a bit -- as a reconnaissance officer, I feel a bit naked without a map in front of me to explain. But we had, of course, a team site at Lima. We had team sites. There was a gun position not far from Lima where we had a position. We had one down in the region of Pale which could only be reached by coming back through Pale. We had one over in Vogosca and we had one at Blazuj. And, of course, these were really team sites because if there was a report of a violation, they weren't co-located with known gun positions. Only one site was actually anywhere near a gun position. So if there was firing, these teams would deploy or they would be on parole already and they would be at different areas where we expected firing to take place or where there was trouble or where they could undertake a patrol. Does that answer the question or do you want more elaboration?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is fine, sir. During the course of your tour of duty in Sarajevo, did the number of observation posts on either side of the line increase?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. The -- I changed dramatically the situation in Sarajevo after the ceasefire. I changed its orientation because, after the ceasefire, we no longer were observing the fall of shot into Sarajevo. We tried to put ourselves in a position to observe the front line better, to act as a buffer in those cases where the UN could not provide troops, in other words, separate the two parties. We set ourselves up in team bases where we could more easily patrol the total exclusion zone which you will remember, from other witnesses perhaps, was 20 kilometres, a 20-kilometre radius from Sarajevo. And, of course, we tried to get into areas that had been potential hot spots in the previous months, where we had not been allowed access in the previous months, and to establish an UN presence. So I had a total, at peak, of 29 observation posts or team sites. I also had to deploy teams to some areas that were slightly remote from Sarajevo, for example, a weapons site south of Pale where there was no UN troops available to man. And I used -- I provided -- I put my team base in that weapons collection point and then they used it as a patrol base. And this was due to the shortage of resources. I did not like having my military observers tied down in this, what I could consider a static task. Does that clarifies that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: And I must say, it changed, it evolved. If we had trouble spots, for example, when we were moving guns into the weapons collection points, we had team bases at locations which we later closed. Again, by resources, I had a peak of 223 people. When the peace came in Central Bosnia, I lost military observers. As I lost military observers and vehicles, I closed observation posts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was actually my follow-up question. You said, at peak, you had 29 observation posts?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many observation posts were up and running when you departed Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I had 17 team sites or observation posts when I left, and I had reorganised the structure because I was trying to have UNMOs able to work on both sides of the line and to be intimately familiar with the people in their little sector on both sides. I had broken Sarajevo into five districts and I created teams that were -- worked a district which included both Bosnians and Bosnian Serbs. So instead of a Papa and a Lima team, I had five -- 17 OPs spread among five teams. No longer Papa and Lima teams, but teams which would deal with both sides, and in some cases, they had access across the front lines, which was not possible in the months before February. I mean, there was very restricted crossing. But this was -- and it also was made necessary by the demands. The ceasefire violations were happening at a very low level and at the battalion level, and the military observers had to be right on top of this and have intimate knowledge and relationships with the battalion commanders involved. They had to know the ground, the trench line, and changes. Does that answer that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is fine. Do you recall the approximate date or month that you put this realignment plan into effect?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. It took place over May and I phased it. I tried it first in the most sensitive area, Grbavica, because the -- in Grbavica, a typical -- for the edification of the Court, a typical situation, there was -- the front line was a building we called the red house, and it was about six storeys, and they were fighting through the walls. So they were punching holes through the walls and fighting each other through the walls. And we wanted the UNMOs that dealt with this situation to come into the building from either side, i.e. from the Bosnian side or from the Serb side. So that is the kind of situation we tried to resolve in Grbavica, that an UNMO would not have to go all the way around to come in the Bosnian side of the building because we wanted them to be able to cross at wherever the duties required to see both sides of the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pilipovic hasn't the translation, and I see that you are going too fast. I hear there was shootings through the holes and it was shooting through the walls, so it is too quick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you have to keep your speed down again. I also notice -- I also notice, Mr. Southwell [sic], that if a very short question is asked of you, you tell us a lot, both in relation to the question but also things that are not directly related to that question. Since we have some restraints of time here as well, I will ask you to listen very carefully to the question and I might ask Mr. Mundis, of course, if you find all the elaborations of such relevance that you would not interrupt the witness, of course, you are entirely free to do so. But some more guidance might assist both the Prosecution with its wishes, also, for the return of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It is a bit difficult in light of speaking the same languages with the pause between question and answer to jump in. But I will try to do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, can you please describe for the Trial Chamber how the UNMOs reported information to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Up until February, the UNMOs reported to their team leader, either on the Papa and Lima side. Their reports for the day were consolidated so as to reach -- so as to reach my headquarters in time for us to prepare report at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was done with the information that was put in these reports?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: The information was consolidated into an UNMO Sarajevo sit-rep which was sent -- sit-rep, situation report, which was sent to Sector Sarajevo, to BH Command, to Zagreb, and then occasionally to New York.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe in general terms the situation on the ground in Sarajevo upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It is very complex situation to give a short answer. One incident happened just as I arrived, which interfered with my hand-over. One of the observation posts was evacuated, Papa 3, because it was anticipated that perhaps it would certainly be shelled heavily and maybe the repulse of a Bosnian attack by the Serbs would carry over the fighting into that general area. The evacuation was done by French, and the Bosnian 10 Hill Brigade took the APC for two days, with the possessions of the people. So it was a very hectic time. At the same time, there was an attack ongoing on the Pale road. So it -- and there was shelling, and I think the Court has access to sit-reps that were sent during this period, but you will see that there was a range of shelling. So in November -- do you want me to carry on month by month? I don't want to take up the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is fine. Let me just ask a couple of questions. You say there was shelling. Can you characterise the nature of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Do you want for the month of October when I arrived or for the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time period when you arrived.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: The shelling was generally into Sarajevo. But I can't be specific. In the area, I was more focused on Papa 3 and there was definitely shelling on Papa 3. You should be aware that the shelling was coming from the Bosnian Serb side, but the Bosnians had also located mortars not too far from the location of Papa 3. There was an attack ongoing onto the Pale road which we couldn't monitor. We weren't allowed close enough to the front lines. It was severe enough that my predecessor had evacuated the OP. In fact, it was ongoing when I arrived in Sarajevo. The aftermath of this evacuation, trying to get our people back into this position, the French trying to get their APC back, the missing kit from the APC, this was a big disruption for the first week that I was there. Moreover, I had taken the time to visit all my OPs at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, shortly after your arrival in Sarajevo, visiting the Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of that visit?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I intended to make, as I had already done in Sarajevo, a courtesy visit on the senior Serb commander in the area, who was General Galic, the corps commander. I had already met his opposite number in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at Lukavica barracks, did you meet with the Lima team leader?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I met with the Lima team leader and he, of course, had to give me a briefing as well. And I, in fact, made arrangements through him to visit all of his OPs and to spend time at each of the observation posts and team sites in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon your arrival in Sarajevo, who was the leader team leader?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It was a Danish team leader, Jan Pedersen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Major Pedersen introduce you to any officers of the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: The main officer I remember meeting in my initial visit to Lukavica was then Major Indjic. He is now a Colonel. I did not meet the corps commander and I don't recall meeting any of the other staff, although I have met Marko, who was a security officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met Major Indjic or when Major Indjic was introduced to you, do you recall what his duties and responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Major Indjic was the liaison officer for General Galic and his headquarters, and my understanding was they wanted him to be the main point of contact for us when we tried to deal with the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of issues would you be dealing with or what would be the subject matter of the issues you would be dealing with at the Lukavica barracks headquarters?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: This would be the complete range, anything that I would want to raise, from getting approval for location of a team site, to dealing with ongoing artillery fire on the city, to an incident involving UN personnel where our people had been shot at by snipers or our accommodation in the city had been shelled. Those are some of the range of some of the issues. Also I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am apologising. There is another small problem of translation. I do not see here on page 20, 18 in French, I think the French is not correct. I think it is a question of setting up a site. It is just perhaps a small matter which I would like to bring to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. You may continue your answer. You were, at least as I can see on the screen, dealing with ongoing artillery fire on the city, incident involving UN personnel where people had been shot at by snipers or accommodation in the city had been shelled. Those are -- some in the range of some of the issues.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you wish me to elaborate on more?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will leave that to Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One issue I should bring up is freedom of access was always an issue on both sides. We were prohibited from going into areas by both parties which prevented us obviously from seeing what we wanted to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "ongoing artillery fire on the city," what was that in reference to?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: This would be where, for example, my Papa sent a team site which was in the centre of the city, not far from the market. It would be getting -- be subject to shelling. And we might have, for example, UN vehicles parked outside soft-skin UN vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also, as part of your duties, liaise with Major Indjic with respect to civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. The normal procedure was, we would pass a message to Lukavica if there were -- if shelling was taking place in the city and the duty staff there would notify Major Indjic. If we wanted to raise the level of response to indicate we wanted a higher degree of attention paid to this, then we would ask Major Pedersen to contact Indjic and make sure he understood that we wanted something done about this. Finally, the next level was for me to personally go to Lukavica to say that this was -- we would -- you know, this would stop. Normally, we wouldn't go that far and I can't relate whether the fire stopped because of our intervention or other factors, in most cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you about your meetings with Major Indjic in a moment. First, let me ask you if you recall where the Lima team headquarters was located in the Lukavica barracks.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It was located directly in the same office building that General Galic had an office and that Indjic had an office. And our operations room and main office for the Lima team was directly opposite the office or the waiting room where I would normally find Indjic and the captain he had working for him. And adjacent to our office OP centre was a room with a sleeping quarters and facilities for cooking meals. So the team actually lived there for a period of time. They also had a house nearby where they, when they weren't on duty, they could sleep. It was more elaborate. We permitted the team because Mr. Major liked to orient his team. He had some training for them before they actually got integrated into his team. So they had a larger house nearby as well. But there was accommodation and operations right opposite Indjic's office, in the same building as General Galic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many times during your tour you met with Major Indjic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I -- every time I passed the headquarters and had reason to go and see my people, I would also - as a courtesy, if nothing else - stop to see Major Indjic. Generally, I had also had issues to bring up, and before I would leave my own headquarters, I would review any issues I might have to bring and discuss with Major Indjic. And it could range again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am really -- I really apologise, but a whole paragraph has been forgotten in the French translation because the French interpreters are not able to keep up. From the sentence 23 where Mr. Pedersen is mentioned, none of this is on the screen. I apologise truly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Thank you for your assistance, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologise for the French booth, but I have to say this. Let us repeat from that point. It is a gap. And I apologise again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Thomas, would you please repeat on from where you talked about Mr. Pedersen, that he would prefer to have that house nearby for the people who were not on duty and reasons why he wanted to have that house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, as well, for being a little too fast. Mr. Pedersen had a larger accommodation in a house nearby because he wished to have space for the new team members for the Lima team, all of the seven OPs -- this is in addition to what I previously said -- so that they could be briefed and brought into his team without having them in General Galic's headquarters. And so he had a larger accommodation. The accommodation in the Lukavica barracks proper was for the team that was working there, although, when things were difficult, Mr. Pedersen himself used to stay there the whole time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, do you recall approximately how many times, during the course of your tour of duty in Sarajevo, you met with Major Indjic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I would say I met him -- I was there 365 days. I must have surely seen him 150 times. Surely, 100 times, anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier a ceasefire. Do you recall the approximate date the ceasefire took effect?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I think it was implemented on 9 or 10 February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to the time period between your arrival in Sarajevo and the date of the ceasefire. During that roughly five-month period, how frequently would you meet with Major Indjic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I would certainly see him, at minimum, once a week and I would say more often than that. I mean twice a week for sure. It would depend on what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet with Major Indjic in his office in the Lima team OPs room or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It depended on what we wanted to talk about, but normally I met in his office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the contents of Major Indjic's office?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I was more interested in what he was going to say and focused on maps and so on that he might have about. But he had sort of a waiting room. We would go in. Normally, we would be spreading a map out on a coffee table and discussing, using the map as the centre of our discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the topic matters that you discussed with Major Indjic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I think I suggested these already. But I would be talking about freedom of movement, I would be talking about shelling, I would be talking about sniper activity, I would be talking about UN people being shot at, and asking him to give us guarantees of security in certain areas. That would be some of the things that we would talk. I might be trying to get his assistance in getting a convoy somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you elaborate upon what you might have said to Major Indjic about shelling?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I am sure I would have raised the issue if one of our OPs -- if the shelling had landed close to our OP, for example, Papa 5 or our Papa headquarters. I would have pointed out to him that he knew where these locations were, that he knew that UN personnel were there, and that they were still firing close. By "close," I mean almost hitting. I should elaborate for the benefit of the Court, when one of my teams was fired upon, I went to the belligerent involved and personally asked to see the corps commander so I could complain about one of my team sites being fired upon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if you also had discussions with Major Indjic with respect to shelling of civilians?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. Although the majority of these kinds of discussions would have been passed if they were through the telephone as initial, trying to get it stopped, or to Major Pedersen. And normally by the time I would be seeing Indjic, there should have been no shelling happening. In fact, maybe I wouldn't have been able to move out if there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any discussions that you had with Major Indjic with respect to sniper activity?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I think we probably discussed -- and I can't recall any specific incident -- we probably discussed sniper activity in relationship to OPs, to sniper alley, and to reducing tension in areas. I must admit, in the time frame you asked me to talk about, sniper activity was secondary to dealing with shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall on approximately how many occasions you spoke with Major Indjic with respect to shelling of civilians?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I couldn't make a guess as to how much. I would say that it came up as an issue quite often when I was there. It would be one of the agenda items that I would have marked in my little book to talk to him about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many occasions you spoke to him about snipers targeting civilians?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: This became an issue after the ceasefire when it appeared to be the response of the Serbs to Bosnian violations of digging. The Bosnians would improve their trenches or perhaps even tunnel, and the Serbian response was to initiate sniper activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning to your discussions with Major Indjic prior to the ceasefire, do you recall Major Indjic's response on any of the occasions that you met with him with respect to your protests?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I am not convinced that our protest had any impact whatsoever. The firing stopped, but I am not sure that it didn't stop because of other considerations. And if the firing continued, the force commander, the UN force commander - actually, the deputy force commander - was responsible for sending a formal note. So I am sure there is a record of some of the formal notes that were sent. And you must be aware as well, that other -- the UN military also reported shelling an initiated complaints, such as when the Egyptian battalion was shelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "UN military," are you referring to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: UNPROFOR, yes. That was the only UN military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time period prior to the ceasefire, on how many occasions did you meet with the corps commander, General Galic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Once. Prior to the ceasefire, I only met General Galic once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make more than one request to meet with the corps commander, General Galic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. I, from the day of arrival, I tried to meet him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom did you address these requests for meetings?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: The requests were made through Major Indjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Major Indjic explain to you why he was unable to get you an appointment with the Corps Commander, General Galic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I received a variety of explanations. My team commander was also trying to make arrangements for me to meet. There was also some excuse, which ranged from being out of town, to being unavailable, to some kind of operation ongoing or whatever. I think my actual meeting was with him in the hall, where he couldn't avoid me because I was coming in unexpectedly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "meeting with him in the hall," you are referring to General Galic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the reasons you gave to Major Indjic for wanting a meeting with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: The first meeting was, I like to know who I am dealing with. I make it a policy when I am in these kind of operations to know who the people are that I work with. And he was a key player and I didn't know him. And I don't consider I really know him today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you consider it important for the fulfillment of your duties to meet with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I raised the issue not only with Indjic, I raised it with the French commander as well, that I was not seeming to get access that I needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the meeting or encounter that you had with General Galic in the hallway?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It was just a courtesy. I wanted to meet the General and I wanted to indicate who I was so he knew me, so he knew the face behind the activity that I was doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date of this encounter?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I can't remember. It happened after Christmas. And it happened obviously from Christmas to February the 6th or 7th, when the market massacre took place; it seems like a blur of activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the duration of that meeting or encounter?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It was just a -- that is why I think it was a chance encounter. I can't remember any of the details, and it was just a courtesy acquaintance, get-acquainted meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss any of the substantive issues that were on your agenda to discuss?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No. It wouldn't be my practice normally. I like to meet the man and then raise -- ask to see him again to raise the issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this chance encounter or this encounter in the hallway, did you have any other meetings with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. After the ceasefire, the French commander took me as one of his military advisors and I had at least 7 to 10 meetings in the space of two weeks immediately after the ceasefire. And I was present in the same meeting with the French commander and with General Galic and I had several opportunities to talk directly about matters of substance, mainly related implementation of the ceasefire, location of weapons collections points, freedom of access for us to do our job and inspecting the total exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During any of the meetings that you had with General Galic, was the subject of civilian sniping, sniping of civilians or shelling of civilians discussed?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, but, of course, the market massacre was the whole reason that we were having those meetings, and the ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anything that General Galic said in these meetings with respect to the market massacre?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No. I can't remember anything that was said at the meetings, nor did we raise the issue of who was responsible. Because by this time, a UN special investigating time had been created and dispatched to Sarajevo to look into the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time of the -- from the time of the signing of the ceasefire until your departure from Sarajevo, did the ceasefire hold throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I can't give a short answer to that. And I should say that there was no signing. General Rose announced in front of the media and the face of the two parties that there had been too much signing already, and that he expected at 12 noon the next day that both sides would stop firing, and if anybody shot after that, the media there would know which side was not adhering to the ceasefire. So there was actually no physical signing, which actually created a problem for us in some ways because there was no document. Do you want me now to go into some detail about the ceasefire holding? I can give a general impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would prefer a general impression, sir.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: The first two weeks of the ceasefire, I think was a missed opportunity. The soldiers in the ground, in the trenches, on both sides - and I visited the trenches - wanted to stop fighting. And if you look, I had no requirement to start creating a summary of sniper activities for the remaining days in February because there was very little. But, in March, the first casualties started. We had complaints from the Serbs that the Bosnians were improving their positions. And, indeed, from personal experience, I can tell you I saw trenches that moved forward. Also, the Bosnians and the Serbs both killed each other with sniper fire. So what had been very good in the ground for the guys in the trenches was changing because of the nature of sniper warfare. Several measures were instituted by General Rose, but for example, the bus to go from Sarajevo to Visoko, to create an outlet for people from Sarajevo, required convoy escort throughout the whole time of my remaining tour. This was a confidence-building measure, and it is true the lines were more open for UN. But another incident that showed that the tension was coming back: Initially, I could go for the first time from Sarajevo to Pale on the road that had been intended to connect those two places. But then, for a number of excuses, mines appeared again, roadblocks appeared again, and we were once more stuck with going around. And we, the UN, and the belligerents appeared to be moving towards a conflict again. And I -- the sniper and the defensive positions, there was -- it became worse and worse, except for isolated incidents. And when I found in certain areas that I was able to arrange a ceasefire, such as during the World Cup, and perhaps it is appropriate to use that as an example, a very sensitive area near the airport, the two battalions, we found by putting military observers there -- I don't want to take too much of the Court's time on this, but it illustrates the point. The two battalions wanted to watch the World Cup, and so did their soldiers. We got a ceasefire, but a sniper bullet killing a football player on one of the battalion teams got them all shooting again, and I feel that the sniper, the orders of the snipers, came from higher authorities. So the higher authorities, in my humble opinion, were not prepared to make the ceasefire work, but the soldiers on the ground wanted it, and slowly but surely -- when I left, we initially -- in March, I was able to send patrols to exactly the front lines and to patrol the entire front line, walk it. We did walk it. In June, when I tried to do the same, to see what changes had been made to the front line, I was denied access by both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, if you could fine a suitable moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just a couple of more questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, in the period until after the ceasefire was arranged until your departure from Sarajevo, what was the level of shelling activity in the city compared to the period prior to the ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: There was no shelling at all from indirect fire weapons. The few reported violations, and I investigated one personally that was in no-man's land, were hand held anti-tank weapons fired in a high trajectory, which created the impression -- would have a similar impact as a mortar. I am talking about an RPG-7 fired at an elevation, or another hand held anti-tank weapon. And the round would travel in an arc and create an explosion similar to a mortar round. But there was no mortar rounds or artillery rounds fired that we could tell determine within Sector Sarajevo into the city. There was some violations from artillery firing from within the total exclusion zone, within the Sarajevo area, but into central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you now very briefly again about sniping activity during that period in -- I believe what you said was, in the first month or so after the ceasefire, there was a dramatic decrease in sniping which then picked up again in the final couple of months in your tenure.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I would ask the Court if they can look at a document which I think has been submitted, but it had a summary of the sniping. I found I had -- after starting on the 1st of March, I found that the sniping had increased to the point that I needed to start creating a summary of who was killing who. And I maintained that summary until the day I left. And from that, you will see a record of the sniping activities. It is similar in form to another document I think that the Court has which I started in December, of recording incoming shells on both the Bosnian and on the Serb side. So both sides had people killed by shells and both sides had people killed by snipers, and I had to start doing this again in March. And I can't recall from the top of my head, but I think the Court could examine that document and see a pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This would be an appropriate time for a break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We will adjourn until 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of the fact that the witness and I both speak the same language and the witness tends to give rather lengthy answers, as the Chamber has already noticed, I am wondering, if it might be appropriate for yourself, Mr. President, to direct the witness to look more in my direction rather than facing the Bench so that I can perhaps give him some indication by hand as to when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis. I don't know whether that would be the proper solution because the witness is informed by the Chamber. So, therefore, I would not like to say, "Just look at the one who questions you," but I and the Chamber has noted the problems you might have. I don't ask you to make a pause if you say, "Mr. Witness, please stop." Now, I will ask his attention that if he hears something alike from your mouth, that he should stop and wait for further questions or guidance. Because, otherwise, he will not return to Canada soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I will instruct the witness to listen carefully, and the pause is not necessary under these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I will attempt to intervene as quickly as possible, and then once he stops, pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you don't overcome the problems, Mr. Mundis, if you give me a signal, I will transfer it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I should also just indicate very briefly before the witness returns, is that I would at this point like to turn to the Rule 70 documents and I would ask that we go into closed session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before doing so, Mr. Ierace asked whether he would have to return in respect of what is now called the "grattage." Could you convey to him that the Chamber asked for either an answer or a written report. What we got, as a matter of fact, was a short answer by Mr. Stamp which was, well, not an answer in the sense that it would explain the reasons of the grattage, and the Chamber would very much like to be informed in more detail on exactly what steps have been taken. Mention was made of correspondence and we would like to be informed rather in detail of dates, et cetera, who was addressed, so that we are in a better position to assess whether the answer that no on knows would finally be an acceptable answer or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would you like those details conveyed in writing or would you like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We would prefer to have them in writing by next Monday. It is dragging along for quite some time now, so it could be prepared for next Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That would be the 3rd of the June, this coming Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This coming Monday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I don't know if this witness has to return to French or English Canada very soon, but what I do know is that the problems facing the French booth come from the fact that they work from the relay and not -- they don't translate directly. So what is important, I think -- I think that is what I have understood according to what I was told by the French booths. It is important that when they see that this witness is speaking too rapidly, it would be important to slow him down. It is his speed that can create problems for the French booth, if I have understood this matter correctly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There seems to be no doubt as to the speed being the cause of the problems. We then now turn into closed session. Private session would not be enough, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, sir, my instructions were closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not my question what your instructions were but whether it would be good enough. But let's just assume for the time being that your instructions were in accordance with the necessity of closed question. There is no one in the public gallery? There is one. Mr. Usher, could you then please assist in bringing the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, we are now in open session again. We take it that the clarification that you give, if you refer to the number of documents, and give your clarification, if they are still needed. Mr. Mundis, I leave that entirely up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can clarify these documents P2055. I can only apologise for what we did at the time, but that should clearly read January for December where it says "period." Because I have checked with the casualty and those sit-reps and Exhibit P2063 should also read January for December where it says "sit-rep." Were those the only documents in question or was there another one? Just let me -- 2051, to confirm again, 2051.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would be the correct date on that one?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: This one, that should be -- also read January. Where it has "December" on the line "period," it should read "January."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those changes would simply be in order to correct what appear to be typographical errors?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thomas. I have a few more documents to show you, sir. I would ask at this time that the witness be shown P2297 and also P2761.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Might the interpreters in the booths also get copies at this time of the documents because we have been working throughout this whole day without any copies of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, I don't know whether you have heard, but the interpreters are asking if there are available copies for them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the documents are being distributed, I will accept responsibility for failing to provide the documents earlier to the interpreters, and I beg their apology for that oversight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, I ask you to first look at P2297. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber who created this document or who compiled the information on this document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I created -- had this document created, to provide me with a summary of the casualties which you saw on the sit-reps or some of the samples of the sit-reps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose for creating this summary document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It was to give me an overview, day by day, during the month, of the casualties on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document begins with December 1993. Do you recall whether you had similar summaries made for that portion of October when you were in Sarajevo, or for the month of November 1993?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No. I arrived in October and they didn't have this kind of procedure. My first two weeks were spent getting to know the different teams and their sites, and it was only early in December that I got around to organising the procedures that I wanted in my own headquarters. And this is one of the procedures I found very useful, to have a summary such as this so that I could take to meetings and describe to people and to brief people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask you to turn please to the fourth page of this document of February 1994.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are no entries after the 7th of February, 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: That is correct. After the market massacre -- the market massacre isn't reflected so I can only assume that it occurred on the 8th. And the casualties for that day were horrendous. I think, if my recollection serves me, 200 or more. And for the rest of February, there was no artillery fire. So the only casualties that would result after that were sniper fire, and as I think I alluded to earlier when you asked me a question about the situation after the ceasefire, initially, there was almost no activity for the first two -- the remaining weeks in February, there wasn't enough casualties to justify keeping this kind of a summary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you two questions to clarify. First: Does this summary which is marked P2297, reflect shelling casualties only or shelling and sniping casualties?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: This document reflects shelling and sniping casualties. It would be based on what had been submitted on the sit-reps. However, it has to be correlated with the sit-reps with care, as the sit-reps were ended at 1800 hours and this would reflect casualties that occurred during the night. And, therefore, there would be some differences between this summary, which reflected evening casualties, and the casualties covered in the two sit-reps, which went from 1800 to 1800. And the duty officer on duty would have had to make a judgment when he made this summary for me, when he was including the casualties of the evening, whether they properly belonged in the 2nd of December or the 3rd of December, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is possible that if you were to compare a sit-rep for a given period with this summary chart, that the numbers might not match?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: They might not match, and my intent wasn't to have this -- this was to give me the feel for the casualties, when they occurred and what dates. And the sit-reps, I could haul out then to compare what I had told the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I draw your attention, Mr. Thomas, to the casualties listed on page four of this document, February 1994, 8-5, which would reflect the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The casualties on the Bosnian side are rather substantial?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: That very -- in fact, might be the date of the marketplace massacre, and thanks for bringing that to my attention. Because I can't think of any other date that we had that tremendous amount of casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I repeat that I ask to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was just about to intervene. Mr. President, can we -- there is a confusion in the French transcript. Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In reference to the summary of casualties for 5 February, 1994, on the Bosnian side, the numbers seem to be rather substantial. Can you recall or explain why the numbers were particularly high on that date?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: My earlier explanation perhaps isn't correct. I -- at first sight, it appears to be the date of the market massacre, but I am not convinced because we had no activities after the market massacre occurred. We had casualties -- we stopped having any casualties. So there is some discrepancy here which, again, I would have to see the sit-reps for those days to reconcile this. Because as far as I am concerned, when the market massacre occurred, basically, we had an end for a period of time to casualties. Unless, in fact, these are bodies that were brought into the morgue which my guys counted and they appeared in the morgue for the first time on those dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to document P2761, can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: This was a document which unfortunately I had to start creating because now we started to have casualties, sniper casualties, on both sides. As you will notice, there are both Bosnian and Bosnian Serb and, indeed, I have the French casualties also recorded. So this was a summary of the casualties. The only thing that is not clear in my mind, whether we in fact originated this in the UNMO headquarters or whether in fact this was a document that originated in the French sector headquarters, and I am not -- my recollection isn't clear on that matter. But this is what this represents, is a summary, a daily summary, of the sniper casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the key at the bottom of this document pertains to the figures listed on the document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: That is correct. Soldiers, we tried to distinguish between soldiers, civilians and, of course, killed, wounded, and then there was a distinction made for females.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you make the determination as to whether or not an individual was a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: The basic characteristic we used, and I should say that this was also used in judging casualties from shelling, was that women and children were assumed, unless otherwise identified, to be not soldiers. The males over a certain age were assumed to be soldiers or possible replacement soldiers because, in Sarajevo and in also on the Serb side, most of the males wore bits and pieces of uniform and, in fact, if they were over the age of 16 or 17, could have basic military training, conscript training, so therefore were suitable to be employed as soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on this methodology, would you expect these numbers to be on the high end, or on the low end?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: In what way do you mean? You mean the number of soldiers reported to be on the high end or the number of civilians?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take the number of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I would say that you would find that most males that we could possibly identify as being 17 or 18, therefore, of draft age, that they would be considered soldiers or possible replacements and they would probably be wearing some military attire. So I would say that perhaps a number of soldiers might be slightly overestimated in the sense that untrained soldiers wouldn't be used if they could avoid it. Although, in Sarajevo at that time, I think they would use them. And that is why we took the conscript age because these guys would have had their basic training so they would know how to use the weapons. Obviously, both sides -- I should make it clear -- both sides used combatants who were not militarily trained and who were under this age. But when you see the body, it is hard to interrogate it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention now to sniping in general. During the time that you were in Sarajevo, based on the information that was reported to you by the military observers, were you able to identify locations where Bosnian Serb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. There seems to be a problem today. It is not perhaps the problem of the booth. Perhaps it is a technical problem. A whole sentence has not been translated, that "it is difficult to interrogate a body." Well, it hasn't been translated at all, and it is not the first time I have noticed this. I can't get up every few minutes, but this time I think it was useful that I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you read it for assistance. Mainly drawing attention to a mistake is accompanied by a few lines of why you are sorry and why it was useful, et cetera. If you do it as short as possible, that would certainly assist. Where we should resume? Perhaps, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you indicate what line has not been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It is exactly the line 6 current page, "When you see the body, it's hard to interrogate."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. The words were not translated: "But when you see the body, it is hard to interrogate it." Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to sniping, during the time you were in Sarajevo and based upon the reports that you received from the military observers, were you able to identify locations where Bosnian Serb army snipers were active?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. We knew of three sites in particular that I can cite, is that there was a tower in the field opposite Lukavica, between the entrance to the Lukavica barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: And -- yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "a tower," what kind of tower?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It was a tower, a part of a church. There was also a site in the School of Theology, Nedzarici, and there was a site in Grbavica that was opposite one of our military observer posts, and we knew this one quite well because there was retaliatory fire. And every time we discovered the location of this sniper post, we would ask the Bosnian Serbs to move it. There was, of course, certain areas in the city, the press named "sniper alley" which contained target areas for snipers. The practice of sniping, of course, once they fire, if there's other snipers active against them, they would move once they'd fired and given away their location. To say there was one or two locations is perhaps misleading. I think that, in the case of sniper alley, there were several locations they used and they moved to. There was no alternative to using the tower location opposite -- the church tower close to Lukavica. They would have no other dominating fire position. So they had to continue using the tower, even though it was known to be the location of a sniper. A similar thing would be said for the School of Theology. It was a structure which allowed sniping, and there was no other good position they could move to, if once -- so they would have to stay there and move back into the building, out of sight, to avoid retaliatory fire or decide to stay and take the retaliatory fire. But on some of the other locations, and this would apply to snipers on both sides, they would fire and try to move to another alternative location that covered the same target area, and some of these positions would offer that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which neighbourhood or part of the city could be targeted by a sniper from the church tower?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: That would be in Dobrinja, the area that was close to the airport. And I think the Court is familiar with that area. I am sure you have seen it many times already on maps from other witnesses. But that area would be targeted. And the School of Theology also targeted that area from the other side.
