If you think -- visualise the Dobrinja area and it's curved like this, and the airport is here, and the tower is here and the School of Theology is in here, Nedzarici, in an area held by the Bosnian Serb. There was a machine-gun located in the School of Theology - and perhaps I'm getting into too much detail - but it could cover the street for a kilometre and-a-half and kill anybody that tried to cross that street. Later, in the period after the ceasefire, we would put a military observer patrol in there to observe this position and then they wouldn't fire while we were present. In the tower, they had a similar control of the streets on the far end of Dobrinja which were close to the Lukavica area. There was an open space there. And my only observations - I was in the School of Theology - but my observation of the tower was limited because I only saw it from within Dobrinja itself. I was never able to get access to see it from the Serb side. I might add that there was also a Bosnian sniper nest in the far end of Dobrinja which could engage targets going into Lukavica barracks. So those two -- I hope those snipers killed a few of each other off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with any geographic formations in or around the city of Sarajevo from which Bosnian Serb army snipers operated?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. There is one which we were -- after the ceasefire, we tried to negotiate a military observer presence called the "Sharpstone." And this took -- this would be an issue which would have started out at a team level because the team in the city where the casualties were occurring wasn't allowed to operate on the Serb side. We would have to have the team that was responsible for that area on the Serb side go around and try to negotiate and then talk to the radio with the team in the city. This is why I tried to change the organisation in May and June of that year. So I often got involved because I could freely cross the line. In the case of Sharpstone, I was able to cross the front line. I met my team on the Bosnian side, I got briefed on the situation, for example, the latest casualties of that day, and they were shooting from that feature. I don't even know the rhyme nor reason of why they picked individuals to be killed. Then I crossed the line, I went up to the Serb position, and it was, in fact, a very well dug-in position and there was no need for any special facilities for the snipers. They could just pick a trench and prepare themselves, shoot, and then move to another trench. And had a very clear view. And this was one of the things that we spent some time negotiating, first at the local level, no luck, and finally it would have been something I would have brought to General Galic's attention at his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "brought to General Galic's attention," how would you do that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, I would bring it to Major Indjic, and that is as far as it went. Although there was indications that we would be, in fact, given an opportunity to put a UN presence there, and that is one of the things that was changed with the air strikes in Gorazde. We lost all the negotiations that we had around the Sarajevo area at that time for these -- a UN presence. I was prepared to send an UN team to live there, to the Sharpstone feature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you now about any complaints or protests --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. This is the fifth time the interpreters are asking me to slow down. I don't know, should I use a different language. Should I say it in Italian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will change to the French channel myself again. And may I just ask you, I mean, it is a very difficult task the interpreters perform, and I know that you don't do it on purpose, but please. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. I realise when I have this information, I want to get it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters say straight away when the speaker is -- when the witness is speaking too fast. Thank you very much. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, you mentioned protests made at the local level. Were there any instances where you made any type of protest or complaint directly to any of the brigade or lower level Bosnian Serb army commanders?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. Normally, it would be done, like in the case of Sharpstone. If, in fact, the initial protest or complaint by my local team commander did not appear to have any impact, in the case of Sharpstone, and I will use it as an example because there was a significant number of casualties from that location, we -- then I would make a visit to the brigade commander. At that particular time, we even had trouble determining which brigade was controlling that position. So we then turned to Colonel Indjic, or Major Indjic as he was at the time, and I certainly would have asked for an interview with General Galic because this position was so important to us. Because this Sharpstone position was so important to us that we needed his intervention to make sure that we got -- I don't recall meeting with General Galic on this topic. I think I may have met with his chief of staff. But what I do remember is that we appeared to have agreement in principle that we could establish a UN presence on the Sharpstone. But this agreement was made very early in April of 1994 and this was overtaken by events after the air strike when my people were taken hostage on the Bosnian side -- Bosnian Serb side, and basically negotiations and everything we had been working for was stopped or put on hold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about other instances where you or any of your personnel spoke directly to brigade commanders with respect to complaints.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. I personally intervened in another situation with the brigade commander at Ilidza because I felt in his case, if we had reached an agreement, there would be no firing or no sniper activity, that this would be respected. And so when his soldiers opened fire one morning after we had an agreed ceasefire, I found out that they had been provoked by the sniper killing -- Bosnian snipers killing three pregnant women. So with the certain brigade commanders, I definitely had the feeling that if they said something would happen, that it would happen, on the Bosnian Serb side. My only caveat to that statement would be they often made it very difficult for me to pin them down to an agreement to anything. So they might not agree to anything after half a day of negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to reach any conclusions with respect to command and control issues based on these meetings in which someone said something would happen and, in fact, it did?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. This may take some time, so I ask the Court to bear with me, in the sense that each of the brigade commanders was different. At the level of the brigade I found the Bosnian Serb commanders were generally ex-JNA, very professional, and with quite a lot of skills which I respected. They had operational and tactical knowledge and they could demonstrate this and they had an understanding of the situations they faced. The soldiers they worked with I would say, for the most part, were Territorial Defence soldiers. So I would say that they had to exert supervision to make soldiers also follow their instructions. And in this -- in the most part, I would say again, they did this in a professional manner, but there were exceptions, because they were not working with a professional. They were working with Bosnian Serbs who had been -- had training and then had been put into the whole defence forces, and the same thing was true on the Bosnian army side, but they had less experience than the Bosnian Serb officers in exerting control. So I expected at the brigade level on the Bosnian Serb side adherence to orders that had been issued by the brigade. Similarly, the Bosnian Serb brigade commanders as professionals were -- took orders from the Bosnian Serb corps commander. I can't recall a single instance where they didn't reflect if it had been the corps commander's direction. It didn't appear that they would object. So I thought that from the General Mladic down, down to the brigade commanders, there was a kind of command and control that I would kind of -- that I expect, for example, in the NATO army, as a general rule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, you mentioned earlier when we were reviewing some documents about the theft of certain UN-owned property.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Sarajevo, were you also aware of UN radios being stolen?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, UN radios were stolen. This is a particularly sore point with me because in Sarajevo itself, radios and diesel fuel which we carried in our vehicles was very valuable. And so whenever I parked my vehicle, and I often travelled alone to visit a team, I had to carry my radios, take them out and take out my cans of fuel, spare fuel, and carried them into the building, otherwise they would be stolen. This is inside Sarajevo. The same thing was true on the Bosnian Serb side, but if we were in the Lukavica barracks, for example, I didn't expect anything to be taken. But out in the rural communities, it could also happen. And it is because both the radios and the fuel were valuable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, do you know or have any first-hand information about what happened to the radios?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: The radios were used by both parties to listen to our radio nets. And I will given an example of both parties using it. My voice was dubbed on Bosnian Serb television, because I was asked about what I was doing on Bosnian Serb television. And it was taken directly from my radio net. To use an example from the other side, to be balanced, one of my liaison officer's, out of courtesy, turned off his radio as he walked in to a Bosnian officer's office, but he heard his name being called on the Bosnian officer's radio. So he obviously had his radio on our frequency and was listening to it and didn't even have the sense to turn it to another frequency as we came in the room. So both sides had, as far as I was concerned, free access to our radio net.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if or do you recall seeing an UN radio in the possession of Major Indjic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I did not see a radio that could be clearly identified as UN. But Major Indjic clearly had a Motorola radio in his possession and it is just a question of the crystals and the frequency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I have to admit that I don't see what the relevance of these questions is, the questions that have to do with radios, whether they belong to the UN or not, and I would like to object to the relevance or rather the lack of relevance of these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I perhaps should respond in the absence of the witness or be allowed a little bit of leeway to ask the witness two or three more questions which I think should make the relevance of this line of questioning quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first of all, the question has been answered. I do not know whether your next question would be on the same subject and we would have to discuss it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I do have perhaps one additional question on the subject. Depending of course upon the answer I receive to that question, there may be one or more follow-up questions as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if we have to deal with a matter that presumably takes more time so, therefore, if you find it of importance to avoid that what is, in your view, irrelevant evidence comes to the Chamber, then we will ask the witness to leave the courtroom. If the objection is such that you do not insist, then we could continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I take the time to confer with General Galic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in order, for your information, the matter of relevance is, first of all, a very practical thing, that we shouldn't raise irrelevant things, but on the other hand, we should not pay more time to discussions on relevance as it would take to hear the irrelevant evidence. Another issue is that it is, especially in jury trials, it is very important that the jury is not faced with any irrelevant information to the case. A Bench trial is perhaps a bit less vulnerable in this view. Please confer with your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence maintains its position, unfortunately. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. Looking at the clock, it is five minutes to 7.00. I take it, Mr. Thomas, that a discussion on the relevance of questions might easily take two or three minutes and then we are at 7.00. Therefore, I assume that after hearing the arguments on the relevance of the issue, we might adjourn until tomorrow. But since it was only one remaining question of Mr. Mundis, would you please stay around. But, if you are not called back into the courtroom, then for you it means that the case is adjourned until 2.15 tomorrow in the afternoon. Thank you very much. If I would not see you any more today, please do not discuss with anyone, not even representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, your testimony. Yes. So either until five minutes or until tomorrow in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis, please respond to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the issue of the relevance of this line of questioning can be stated quite simply. The witness will testify to the fact that information was relayed to him from his military observers at various observation posts on both the Papa and Lima side over the UN radio network. He has also testified that both sides to the conflicts, both parties, were in possession of these radios. The relevance of this information, Mr. President, and again, depending on the answers to the question or questions that the witness may be asked, have to do with whether or not the information being reported by the military observers was in fact being received by the parties to the conflict. In effect, Mr. President, this information is or could be considered a direct form of notice to the accused that the events in question were happening. The Prosecution submits that this line of questioning is relevant for that limited purpose of being another example of a form of notice that was available to the parties, and particularly to the Bosnian Serb army side of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, before further conferring, would you please respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The first thing that surprised me in what Mr. Mundis has told us is that he hasn't told us whether the military -- members of the military used coded language, which is the first thing which one does when there is sensitive information. Members of the military are careful to preserve their information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...whether it surprises you or not is not the issue. The issue is whether or not Mr. Mundis have reasons for the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the second thing is that if we place ourselves that on the principle that two or three radio sets might disappear, were they immediately provided to General Galic. I am certain that General Galic would not admit this was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...seek to establish that as far as the means of communication were concerned, that the communication of the UNMOs could be overheard and therefore information might have come to both parties, but also to the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. That is the entirety of this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. You said you had one more question. If that would be true, we could try to finish it. But if there are any other questions as well, then we will try to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, as I said, I would anticipate one, but of course, depending on the answer or in light of the fact that this witness tends to give lengthy answers, I can't guarantee that we would be done in one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we better adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon.
